messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Train Conductor
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar was 29, a single Middle Eastern train conductor who had spent much of his adult life working long shifts moving between stations, checking tickets, answering questions, and keeping one eye on the platform and the other on the people around him. His problems began after a shift that started like any other and ended with a scene he could not shake. He had been standing in the train aisle near the doors when a passenger a few rows ahead suddenly collapsed after striking a seat divider and then the floor. By the time Omar reached him, there was blood on the man’s forehead and along his sleeve, and the sight of the open wound stayed with Omar with a sharpness that felt almost bodily. Other passengers shouted for help, and someone told him the man was probably going to be fine, but Omar could not take in reassurance the way he used to. What stayed with him most was the combination of the blood, the visible injury, and the cold, damp feel of the train that day as he knelt beside the passenger and tried to help direct people away. The temperature on his own skin at that moment seemed to lodge in memory along with the injury itself, so that afterward a certain chill in the air or the feel of cold metal against his hand could bring the scene back with a force that made his stomach tighten.

In the days that followed, Omar found that images of the man’s wounds came back when he least expected them, especially if he saw blood in ordinary life or passed someone with a fresh cut or bruise. A small nick on a coworker’s hand, a paper cut on a passenger, or a scrape on a child’s knee could stop him for a second longer than it should, pulling him back to the platform and the helplessness of watching someone hurt in front of him. He became uneasy around visible injuries and wounds on others in a way that felt embarrassing and hard to explain, because to him they no longer looked minor or routine. They looked like the first signs of another emergency. Even when friends or coworkers told him he had done enough and that he was safe now, he found it impossible to believe them fully. Their reassurance seemed to reach him only intellectually, not in the place where his fear lived, and he would nod while still scanning the room, still feeling as if he needed to account for every exit, every movement, every possibility that something could go wrong again.

At work, that watchfulness became difficult to hide. Omar remained reliable and continued showing up, but he was no longer able to relax in the same way during a shift. He was superalert on platforms and in crowded cars, constantly checking faces, hands, and the floor, and he watched for signs that someone might fall, bleed, or suddenly need help. That alertness followed him home. Even in his apartment, where nothing was happening, he struggled to let himself drift off because he felt he needed to stay alert. He would lie in bed listening for sounds in the hallway or the building outside, telling himself to rest while keeping part of his attention on the door and the window. The effort left him tired, but sleep still felt like something he had to earn by staying watchful first.

Over time, certain sensations made the memory feel immediate rather than distant. A specific temperature on his skin could catch him off guard, especially if he felt abruptly cold in a draft, touched a metal railing, or stepped into an over-air-conditioned car after being outside. In those moments, he would tense before he had fully understood why, as if his body recognized the setting before his mind could catch up. The same was true when he noticed blood or injuries: he could be fine one second and then suddenly feel pulled into the old scene, his attention narrowing around the sight in a way he could not easily turn off. He began choosing routes and routines that kept him from lingering near anything that might stir those reactions, and he found himself moving through days with a kind of guardedness that left little room for ease. Friends noticed he seemed more distant and keyed up, but what troubled Omar most was not their concern; it was his own private certainty that safety could not simply be accepted because someone else said so.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had been wearing on him for months. He was still working, still functioning, but with less sleep, more tension, and the sense that he was always bracing for the next sign of trouble. He finally came in after a stretch of nights when he could not fall asleep until well past midnight because he kept checking the door and replaying the incident with the injured passenger, then arriving at work already exhausted and on edge. What he hoped for was not to forget what happened, but to stop living as if it were about to happen again at any moment. What frightened him most was how hard it had become to believe in safety, even when his mind knew he was home, off duty, and alone in a room that was supposed to be quiet.
